results.summary: This Wokwi project implements a simple combinational logic circuit that converts the ASCII binary representation of the letter 'A' (0x37) to the letter 'V' (0x56). It has 8 input pins and 8 output pins, and requires no external hardware. The design is described as 'basic (broken) logic', suggesting it may not function correctly. The documentation is minimal, providing only a brief description and a test procedure.

This Verilog design implements an SPI-accessible register map that drives a charlieplexed 8x7 LED display. It also includes auxiliary functions such as PWM, UART, WS2812 waveform generation, LFSR, frequency counting, and ultrasonic distance sensing, which are implemented as space and time permit. The design is tested by using SPI to read and write registers and observing the LED display or serial response. External hardware includes a charlieplexed 7x8 LED display, and the design operates at a 10 MHz clock.

This Wokwi project uses simple logic gates to display the letter 'P' on a 7-segment display when the 8-bit input equals 0x46. It has 8 input pins and 8 output pins, but only some are used. The design requires external hardware including a breadboard, 1.8V power supply, connector wires, an 8-position DIP switch, and a 7-segment display. The documentation notes that when all inputs are zero, the display shows inverted segment states for 'P', which was an unintended but interesting result.

This Wokwi project displays the letter 'L' on a 7-segment display when the input combination 0b00101111 is entered and a Step button is pressed. It has 8 input pins and 8 output pins, though only some are used. The design requires external hardware including a 7-segment display, a push button connected to power, and an 8-bit DIP switch. The documentation is brief and does not provide details on the internal logic implementation.

This Wokwi project implements a 'secret code' detector that outputs the letter 'r' on a 7-segment display when the input bits 10101010 are set on IN0 through IN7. It has 8 input pins and 8 output pins. The design requires external hardware including a DIP switch for inputs and a 7-segment display for outputs. The documentation references the TinyTapeout workshop and provides a simple test procedure.

This Wokwi project implements a large AND gate by connecting multiple AND gates together. It outputs a '1' on a 7-segment display when all 8 inputs are high, and '0' otherwise. The design has 8 input pins and 8 output pins, with the outputs labeled for LCD segments. No external hardware is required. The documentation is minimal, describing only the basic function and test procedure.

This Wokwi project uses a string of D flip-flops to create a circular LED illumination pattern on a 7-segment display. It has 8 output pins, with 7 used for the display segments, and operates at a 3 Hz clock. The design requires external hardware including a clock source, a button, and a 7-segment LED display. The documentation is very brief and notes that a reset may be needed to clear the flip-flops if more than one segment is illuminated.

This Verilog design converts a 7-LED APA102 (SPI-style) data stream to a WS2812-compatible single-wire output. It also outputs a continuous UART signal transmitting 'Arglius Barglius' at approximately 115200 baud. The design is tested by connecting an SPI driver to the inputs and a string of at least seven WS2812 LEDs to the output, with level shifters likely needed due to the 1.8V operation. The documentation details the protocol handling, including start/stop conditions and ignoring the APA102 intensity byte, and notes that the WS2812 output module is adapted from another Tiny Tapeout submission.

This Wokwi project is described as exploring Wokwi and GDS, with inputs determining outputs. It has 8 input pins and 8 output pins, and requires no external hardware. The documentation is extremely minimal, stating only that changing inputs changes the output. There is insufficient information to determine the specific function or purpose of the design.

This Wokwi project is titled 'joes-first-tiny-tapeout' and described as 'does nothing... yet'. It has 2 input pins and 1 output pin, and the documentation states that it doesn't actually work yet. The test procedure is to toggle inputs and see outputs toggle, but the design is incomplete. External hardware includes buttons for inputs and an LED for output.
